name: LL-37
route: Applied to ulcers in trials; unapproved injections sold online
status: Not FDA-approved; FDA flagged immunogenicity, tumor-promotion and reproductive concerns
mechanism: The body's own antimicrobial peptide: disrupts microbial membranes and signals immune and repair cells; in excess it can drive skin inflammation

article.summary: LL-37 is the human body's own cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide. Topical leg-ulcer trials gave mixed results, while injected use is unapproved and the FDA cites immunogenicity and tumor concerns.
article.takeaway: LL-37 is the only cathelicidin made by humans, a 37-amino-acid peptide that kills microbes and signals to immune and repair cells.[^1] In chronic leg ulcers, topical LL-37 looked promising at lower strengths in a 34-patient first-in-human trial,[^2] but the larger 148-patient phase 2b trial found **no significant improvement overall**, with a possible benefit only in a post hoc subgroup of large ulcers.[^3] Excess LL-37 is also implicated in disease: it helps trigger the interferon surge in psoriasis[^4] and promotes inflammation in rosacea.[^5] The FDA says it lacks the safety information to judge compounded LL-37 and notes animal findings of possible tumor promotion and harm to male reproduction.[^6]
glance: Not approved; no approved LL-37 product exists
Studied as a topical wound-healing drug; sold online as an immune peptide
Applied to ulcers in trials; unapproved injections online
Two randomized topical trials; otherwise mostly lab and animal work

blocks.text: The body stores LL-37 inside a larger precursor, hCAP18, and cuts out the active piece when needed. LL-37 folds into a helix with one water-loving and one fat-loving face, which lets it bind to and disrupt microbial membranes. It also acts as an 'alarmin': it helps orchestrate immune responses, can both raise and limit inflammation, promotes new blood vessels and wound healing, and may help clear abnormal cells.[^1]
That wide repertoire is the problem for any 'immune-boosting' pitch. The same peptide that helps repair skin can also push inflammation.

rows: 34 people with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers, 4-week treatment phase
Healing rate about 6-fold (0.5 mg/mL, significant) and 3-fold (1.6 mg/mL, not significant) that of placebo; no benefit at the highest strength; no safety concerns[^2]
No significant healing benefit overall; benefit in a post hoc subgroup with ulcers of 10 cm2 or more; well tolerated[^3]
LL-37 binds self-DNA and triggers interferon production in psoriasis;[^4] rosacea skin has high, abnormally processed cathelicidin[^5]

blocks.text: No controlled human trial of injected LL-37 for immune support, infection or any wellness goal was found. Claims for that use rest mainly on cell and animal studies.

items: **Immunogenicity:** the FDA says compounded LL-37 may pose a risk of an unwanted immune reaction for certain routes of administration, along with peptide-related impurities and difficulty characterizing the ingredient.[^6]

**Tumors and fertility:** per the FDA, nonclinical research suggests detrimental effects on male reproduction and that LL-37 can be protumorigenic in some tissues. The agency lacks enough safety information to know whether it would harm humans.[^6]
**Inflammatory disease:** LL-37 drives skin inflammation in psoriasis and rosacea, so adding more is a theoretical concern for people with these or other autoimmune conditions.[^4][^5]
**More is not better:** in the first ulcer trial the highest strength did no better than placebo while lower strengths helped.[^2]
**Gray-market quality:** products sold as research peptides are unapproved. Identity, purity, sterility and endotoxin content are not verified.

blocks.text: LL-37 is not FDA-approved. It had been listed among compounding substances raising significant safety concerns; the nominations were withdrawn, and the FDA's page (current as of April 22, 2026) now lists it as 'nominated but withdrawn' while repeating the concerns above.[^6] Withdrawal does not make compounding allowed: LL-37 appears on none of the FDA category lists updated May 14, 2026,[^7] and it was not on the agenda of the July 23-24, 2026 advisory meeting.[^8]

Anti-doping: LL-37 is not named on WADA's 2026 Prohibited List, but unapproved substances in development fall under category S0 (non-approved substances), prohibited at all times. LL-37 appears to fit that description, so athletes should check before using any product.

LL-37 is a fascinating natural peptide with double-edged biology. The only controlled human trials are topical ulcer studies with mixed results. Injected use is unproven, unapproved and flagged by the FDA for safety unknowns, and gray-market vials add quality risks.

evidence.label: Limited: mixed topical trials; injections untested
evidence.text: Two randomized topical trials gave a promising small result and then a mostly negative larger one,[^2][^3] while injected use has no controlled human data and the FDA calls the safety information insufficient.[^6]

faq.a: It kills microbes in lab tests, but no LL-37 product is approved to treat infection. Antimicrobial action is only one of its many functions in the body.[^1]

faq.q: Can LL-37 help with wound healing?
faq.a: Topical LL-37 has been tested in leg ulcers, with a promising small trial and a larger one that missed its main goal.[^2][^3] That does not support injecting it.

faq.q: Why does the FDA worry about it?
faq.a: The agency cites possible immune reactions, impurities that are hard to characterize, and animal findings of possible tumor promotion and harm to male reproduction, with too little human safety data.[^6]
